title: The mind comes first (1–2)
hookLine: all that we are is the result of what we have thought; pain follows an evil thought as the wheel follows the ox
last: THE DHAMMAPADA — THE PATH, IN VERSES.

lines: AN OX CART ON A DIRT ROAD.
THIS IS HOW YOUR LIFE WORKS.
cards: An ox cart on a dirt road in ancient India. The ox leans into the yoke and steps forward. Behind it, the heavy wooden wheel turns and follows, rut by rut, wherever the ox goes.
The wheel has no say. It can't choose a different road. Everyone in the Buddha's world had watched that a thousand times.
And the first verse of the Dhammapada takes that ordinary sight and says: this is how your life works.

teach.h: VERSE ONE: THE WHEEL FOLLOWS THE OX.
teach.b: Here is verse one in Max Müller's English: “All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts. If a man speaks or acts with an evil thought, pain follows him, as the wheel follows the foot of the ox that draws the carriage.”

teach.h: VERSE TWO: THE SHADOW THAT STAYS.
teach.b: Verse two is its twin, the same shape with one change: if someone speaks or acts with a pure thought, “happiness follows him, like a shadow that never leaves him.”
That's why chapter one is called the twin verses: the wheel and the shadow, pain and happiness, mirroring each other. Müller's opening line is well-known, but the Pali is even more direct.

teach.h: THE PALI: MIND GOES BEFORE ALL.
teach.b: Roughly: mind goes before all things; mind is their chief; they are made by mind. Mind comes first. Speech and action follow, and they carry the quality of the mind they came from.
The old commentary tells a story for verse one.

teach.h: THE BLIND MONK: NO INTENT, NO FAULT.
teach.b: A blind monk named Cakkhupala walked up and down one night and stepped on many insects. Other monks were shocked: he'd killed living things. The Buddha said no.
He didn't see them, and he didn't intend it. There was no evil thought behind the step. For this tradition, what matters is the intention an act comes from.
That's why the verse starts with the mind, not the deed. This isn't a promise that thinking happy thoughts fixes everything. It's closer to a warning, and an invitation.
What you set going in the mind gets pulled along behind you.
And you can watch the ox before the wheel starts to turn.

how: The opening verses of the Dhammapada are among the most often chanted and memorized Buddhist verses; teachers use them to explain that intention (cetana) shapes action and its results.

o: with the mind stilled before the meditation begins
with the mind going first, ahead of words and deeds
a mind that follows wherever the senses lead it

games.q: match the pieces of verses one and two.
p: the blind monk who stepped on insects

s: the Dhammapada says that thinking happy thoughts fixes everything
it says what the mind sets going follows you; it's closer to a warning and an invitation.
in the commentary, the Buddha said the blind monk wasn't at fault for the insects
he didn't see them and didn't intend it; intention is what counts.
the Pali says, roughly, mind goes before all things
Müller's 'all that we are is the result of what we have thought' is a looser, well-known rendering.

games.q: a blind monk has stepped on insects in the dark. the other monks want him blamed for killing. you're the Buddha. what do you say?
o: he broke the precept; he's at fault.
he didn't see them or intend it; there's no fault.
games.why: in the commentary the Buddha clears him: no intention to kill, no evil thought, so no evil deed.

practice: Let the breath find its own pace, and watch for the ox: when a thought comes, a worry, a plan, a memory, notice what it does to your mood before you're carried off, a tightening chest, a softening face, a small lift or a small sinking.
You don't have to change anything; just see the thought step forward and feel the wheel of your mood begin to follow. Then come back to the breath and wait for the next one.

wordCard.voice: Manopubbangama. Having mind as forerunner: the Dhammapada's first two verses, where mind goes before all, and words and deeds follow, like a wheel or a shadow.

orig.note: Pali: 'having mind as their forerunner,' the first word of the Dhammapada.

carryVoice: Your line: the wheel follows the ox. Mind first; the rest follows. See you tomorrow.
